author: dkarl
cardQuote: Google Wave will do well if it usefully aggregates many different modes of communication, but if it attempts to unify them then it will be socially unworkable, a total flop.
quote: What is "flexibility" from a technical point of view is "ambiguity" from a social point of view. Is the conversation real-time or only potentially real-time? IM is a real-time conversation, like two people speaking. E-mail is not. A single protocol and interface for both means people will be constantly confused about each other's intentions. I like the idea of combining and persisting all communications about a single topic, but in the screenshots it looks like all Wave messages look the same. "Draft" mode vs. keystroke mode provides a clue, but what if I don't see the message arrive? What if I have a real-time conversation with somebody, and then five minutes after it ends, one of us posts another message? We have to add some kind of comment indicating whether it is intended as a continuation of the previous conversation, the beginning of a new real-time conversation, or a one-off message (with the sender perhaps not available to chat at the moment.) Everything that is currently implicit in the mode of communication (email, IM, etc.) and in mode-specific indicators (IM status, etc.) will now have to be communicated explicitly. That seems like a big step backwards. Google Wave will do well if it usefully aggregates many different modes of communication, but if it attempts to unify them then it will be socially unworkable, a total flop.
storyTitle: Google Wave Drips With Ambition. A New Communication Platform For A New Web.
outcome: Google stopped developing Wave in August 2010, about 15 months after it was announced.
outcomeDetail: Wave combined email, chat, wikis and real-time editing in one protocol, but users found it confusing and slow. Google open-sourced parts of it.
note: The comment predicted that merging incompatible communication modes would create social confusion and make Wave a flop.

author: intellectronica
cardQuote: Is Google becoming the new Microsoft? Not in the evil sense, but in the lame me-too products that rely on brute force (their huge install base) and no innovation to hopelessly try to compete sense.
quote: Is Google becoming the new Microsoft? Not in the evil sense, but in the lame me-too products that rely on brute force (their huge install base) and no innovation to hopelessly try to compete sense.
storyTitle: Google Buzz
outcome: Google Buzz was discontinued in 2011 after privacy complaints and a class-action settlement.
outcomeDetail: Buzz launched inside Gmail in February 2010 and immediately exposed users' contacts; Google settled a privacy lawsuit and later shut the product down. Its failure became a cautionary tale for Google social products.
note: On launch day, the comment called Buzz a me-too product that relied on Google's install base rather than innovation.

author: noarchy
cardQuote: So wouldn't it simply be a matter of time before they either cut some sort of deal with the RIAA, or get shutdown completely?
quote: I can't imagine that this will hold up, in the long run. Torrent sites get taken down without even hosting actual content, the way that Grooveshark does. So wouldn't it simply be a matter of time before they either cut some sort of deal with the RIAA, or get shutdown completely?
storyTitle: Grooveshark's new Javascript/HTML interface
outcome: Grooveshark shut down on April 30, 2015, after settling copyright lawsuits with major labels.
outcomeDetail: A New York court found the company liable for copyright infringement; the settlement required it to shut down and hand over its assets. The service had operated for nearly a decade in a legal grey zone.
note: Four years before the shutdown, the comment predicted that a service built on unlicensed content would either strike a deal or be shut down.

author: mrshoe
cardQuote: My guess is that Color will see a similar fate. It's unlikely you'll build a great social photo sharing application if that's not your primary focus.
quote: I remember attending a Startup School talk wherein Max Levchin explained that Slide wasn't a "pimp my MySpace" company, but rather a data mining company using MySpace widgets as the trojan horse. So, Nguyen isn't the first serial entrepreneur to receive loads of funding based on his reputation and attempt to exploit the trend du jour to mine data from the masses. We all saw how well that worked out for Slide. My guess is that Color will see a similar fate. It's unlikely you'll build a great social photo sharing application if that's not your primary focus.
storyTitle: At least now we know why Color really got that funding
outcome: Color's $41M launch flopped, the app was overhauled and then sold to Apple in 2012; the original product did not survive.
outcomeDetail: Color launched a location-based photo-sharing app in March 2011 with an unusually large early funding round. Poor reviews and low usage led to a pivot and an acquihire by Apple.
note: The comment compared Color to Slide, another hyped data-mining app that failed, and doubted a photo app built around mining would win users.

author: Killah911
cardQuote: I think the Palm Pre came out with more fanfare, and that didn't turn out that great. If all that really differrentiates HP's tablet from the iPad is the OS, well, quite frankly, it's been done before with the Palm Pre vs. iPhone, with less than flattering results for Palm.

storyTitle: HP TouchPad: Shipping July 1
outcome: HP discontinued the TouchPad in August 2011, about seven weeks after launch, and dumped remaining inventory at $99.
outcomeDetail: The webOS tablet sold poorly against the iPad and HP killed the device along with its webOS hardware line. The fire sale became a defining image of the tablet also-ran era.
note: The comment compared HP's tablet strategy to the Palm Pre's failed fight against the iPhone and predicted the TouchPad would repeat it.

author: h4pless
cardQuote: The glass does not seem to offer much more usability than a smartphone and some duct tape for POV filming.
quote: The idea of Google Glass throws up a few red flags for me... 1) Safety - For some reason thinking about a wireless device strapped in a stationary position on my head brings about heightened concerns of the long term impact of having a electromagnetic field being constantly generated next to my brain... Thinking of horror stories from when cell phones first came out. 2) Safety again - The static position of the glass directly over just one eye makes me think of Steve Martin's downfall in The Jerk. If people are actually wearing these things all the time, I would be concerned with how something that you're constantly having to readjust your focus to see with only one eye may cause a disparity in vision. Of course google could adjust the focus of the glass to be some arbitrary amount of feet out to help with focusing but this seems like it would make for less usable space on that tiny screen and still doesn't address the long term effects of having something statically in the field of vision of only one eye. Both of these may very well have been exhaustively researched and or studied by Google but I think that with the semi-controversial design of this computer, Google might put an "Is It Safe?" section to their marketing material explaining how they've addressed safety concerns. Also, in regards to privacy... As some have mentioned the concerns of being video taped while in the presence of wearing Google glass may prompt a lot of businesses/agencies to disallow their use while in their establishment with signs posted on the door. I don't think jewelry stores or banks or other security prone establishments would want people to so easily be able to comprehensively case the joint with almost complete anonymity. Plus fears of an Orwellian future where everybody is watching everybody for some unknown third-party viewer would not be unfounded. Aside from that, I don't really see the value in Google glass. Perhaps it's just the way they've marketed it.... but it just looks like a cell phone that's been moved to your eye. I really don't need to start seeing POV films of people eating dinner or highlights from a drunken night out. The glass does not seem to offer much more usability than a smartphone and some duct tape for POV filming. Not to mention that I believe Mom may have already patented this idea: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EaHUpWuqNHY (Futurama)
storyTitle: Google Glass
outcome: Google ended the consumer Glass Explorer program in January 2015; the enterprise edition was discontinued in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Glass never became a mainstream consumer product, hampered by price, battery life, social awkwardness and privacy backlash. Google later repositioned it for factory and enterprise work.
note: At launch, the comment questioned the basic consumer value—a phone moved to your eye—and predicted privacy rules would restrict it.

author: 7Figures2Commas

quote: Homejoy charges $20/hour and pays cleaners $12 to $15 an hour[1]. The business model is to undercut rivals[2]. Margin compression appears to be the trend in many of the saturated, highly-competitive personal services markets like home cleaning. Homejoy might have great growth, but investing nearly $50 million in margin compressed sectors seems like a stretch for venture capitalists who have typically invested in high growth, high margin technology companies. The valuation math just gets crazy. What's next? VC-led roll-ups of small, local house cleaning services a la the website roll-ups of the last boom/bubble? storyTitle: Homejoy (YC S10) Raises $38M as It Looks to Expand Beyond Home Cleaning
outcome: Homejoy shut down in July 2015 amid worker-classification lawsuits and reports it could not retain customers.
outcomeDetail: The cleaning marketplace faced lawsuits from cleaners classified as contractors and struggled with repeat bookings. It announced closure and later relaunched under different ownership as Homeaglow.
note: At the time of its $38M raise, the comment questioned the thin margins and the cost of undercutting rivals—problems that defined Homejoy's collapse.

author: cylinder
cardQuote: This Clinkle thing is going to end up being one of the big laughingstocks of the current bubble after it goes down and the bubble bursts.
quote: This Clinkle thing is going to end up being one of the big laughingstocks of the current bubble after it goes down and the bubble bursts. Similar to Pets.com and Webvan and such. This actually gave me a flashback to a website I had completely forgotten about. Does anyone remember FuckedCompany.com?
storyTitle: Layoffs at stealth payment startup Clinkle
outcome: Clinkle never shipped a viable product, shed most of its staff in 2014, and was wound down after raising about $30M.
outcomeDetail: The payments startup raised a celebrated seed round, then suffered layoffs, executive departures and a delayed launch. Investors later sought their money back and the company pivoted into a referral service.
note: Written the same day as the first layoffs, the comment predicted Clinkle would become the bubble's Pets.com—a verdict that held as the company imploded.

author: jaynos
cardQuote: I don't trust the Supreme Court to produce a proper ruling on this one. I assume Aereo will lose.
quote: I don't trust the Supreme Court to produce a proper ruling on this one. I assume Aereo will lose. That said, I don't see how it could be argued that Aereo is breaking any law.
storyTitle: Supreme Court to Hear Aereo Case
outcome: The Supreme Court ruled against Aereo in June 2014, and the company filed for bankruptcy that November.
outcomeDetail: The 6-3 decision held that Aereo's individual tiny antennas still amounted to a public performance. Aereo suspended service, laid off staff, and sold its assets.
note: The comment predicted the legal loss five months before the Supreme Court ruling, even while acknowledging the technology was clever.

author: roc
cardQuote: Before you even sign up it's quite clear that there can't be anything anonymous about this at all.
quote: The identity of the poster is recorded as a core conceit of the system. The app/network is explicitly for sharing secrets between friends . It has to record and store who the secrets came from, in order to determine who their friends are and thus which users to show it to. Before you even sign up it's quite clear that there can't be anything anonymous about this at all. It delivers plausible-deniability at best . Their claims may be fuzzy. People may not be paying too much attention when they sign-up or use it. But they're quite clearly not trying to make an actually anonymous secret sharing site.
storyTitle: Your Anonymous Posts to Secret Aren’t Anonymous After All
outcome: Secret shut down in April 2015, about 16 months after launch, after failing to build a durable anonymous social network.
outcomeDetail: The app raised $35M but faced bullying, privacy backlash, and a clone war with Yik Yak. Co-founder David Byttow announced the shutdown and returned remaining capital.
note: The comment argued the product's core promise was impossible because the system had to record identities to build a friend graph; that contradiction helped sink it.

outcome: Meerkat was pulled from the App Store in October 2016; its team pivoted to Houseparty.
outcomeDetail: Twitter cut Meerkat's access to its social graph in March 2015, and Periscope launched soon after. The company shifted to group video chat and shut down the Meerkat app.
note: The comment placed Meerkat in a long line of failed mobile livestreaming startups and doubted one-to-many mobile video was a mass market.

author: sarchertech
cardQuote: So the CEO dropped out of Standford at 19, started this company, and now she's a billionaire?
quote: So the CEO dropped out of Standford at 19, started this company, and now she's a billionaire? I can see dropping out to found Facebook, but a biotech company? What skills did she have that allowed her to do this, and where did she get the money to hire all the needed PhDs and get through FDA testing? How would she have even gotten access to the equipment and test subjects to prove that her idea was worth investing in outside of an academic setting? The whole thing sounds crazy. Edit: I read Elizabeth Holmes Wikipedia page and it says that when she was a sophomore at Stanford, her Chemical Engineering professor encouraged her to found the company. But I can't find anything about about any breakthroughs she made that warrant the millions in early investments. No one seems to want to talk about what exactly it is they're doing, and they're board of directors has a former Secretary of State, a former Secretary of Defense, and a former Senator. The fact that she's also been able to maintain 51% of this company is also astounding.
storyTitle: Scientists skeptical about Theranos blood test
outcome: Theranos collapsed after a 2015 WSJ investigation, dissolved in 2018, and founder Elizabeth Holmes was convicted of fraud in 2022.
outcomeDetail: The company claimed its Edison devices could run hundreds of tests on a fingerprick of blood; reporting and regulators found inaccurate results. It voided two years of tests, faced SEC and criminal investigations, and dissolved.
note: Months before the WSJ exposé, the comment focused on the absence of peer-reviewed evidence and the gap between the hype and the company's actual, incremental technology.

author: jonknee
cardQuote: Their "automated" method uses more people than a manual operation!
quote: From the video it appears your stereotypical stoned college student working the late shift at Dominos could make pizzas at about 5-10x the rate of that robot assisted assembly line. Their "automated" method uses more people than a manual operation!
storyTitle: Zume, a new startup trying to make a more profitable pizza through robotics
outcome: Zume laid off most of its staff in January 2020, abandoned its robotic pizza business, and shut down in 2023 after raising about $445M.
outcomeDetail: SoftBank-backed Zume struggled with the economics of cooking pizza in trucks and switched to sustainable packaging before running out of runway. It ceased operations in June 2023.
note: The comment punctured the automation narrative at launch: the line needed more people than a normal pizzeria, so the robot story did not translate into labor savings.

author: pdelbarba
cardQuote: I'm calling bullshit. See my calculations in the other thread. ~1600lbs of batteries to hit their specs with current tech and that's VERY generous.
quote: I'm calling bullshit. See my calculations in the other thread. ~1600lbs of batteries to hit their specs with current tech and that's VERY generous. Likely closer to 2k. Lipo capacity going up at 5% a year so 2025 isn't happening unless new battery tech is announced and commercialized in the next 8 years. Also, steering appears to be entirely based on differential thrust. Power loss = uncontrolled descent. Good luck getting that certified...
storyTitle: Lilium – Electric vertical take-⁠off and landing jet
outcome: Lilium filed for insolvency in October 2024 and ceased operations in December 2024 without delivering a production aircraft.
outcomeDetail: The German eVTOL developer raised more than $1B but failed to secure emergency financing. It laid off most staff and stopped flying before any commercial service.
note: The comment attacked Lilium's energy math at launch, calculating that current batteries could not meet its payload and range claims and warning that power loss meant uncontrolled descent.

author: awalton
cardQuote: It just turns out consumers were smart enough to see through the not-so-clever ruse of buying a $400 counterweight to squeeze a package of pre-squeezed juice out of a bag and into a cup.
quote: > but it seems like a roller would be able to provide a more efficient and focused method of squeezing than a press they're using now. Or maybe, just maybe, a screw-driven piston, like many actual juicers have... But let's be completely honest - the machine was always meant to be an expensive countertop device. It looks expensive, it weighs a lot, people will think you spent a lot of money on it even if they don't know how much it'll cost... This is exactly why the engineering staff was told "go nuts" on the hardware design - the more expensive and custom, the better. It does the job of looking like a high-end appliance exactly and precisely, and really nothing more. This company always intended to make its money back selling overpriced juice packs like Keurig, banking on people with more money than common sense buying and using the hell out of these devices for the $14 juice packs. Selling the machines near cost or even as a loss leader was perfectly acceptable, as long as customers had to come back to them for more juice month over month. It just turns out consumers were smart enough to see through the not-so-clever ruse of buying a $400 counterweight to squeeze a package of pre-squeezed juice out of a bag and into a cup...
storyTitle: Why Juicero’s Press Is So Expensive
outcome: Juicero shut down in September 2017, five months after its $400 press became a viral symbol of overfunded Silicon Valley hardware.
outcomeDetail: Reporters showed the juice packs could be squeezed by hand, making the machine pointless. The company cut 25% of staff and lowered prices before shutting down and selling its assets.
note: The comment saw through the razor-and-blades economics: customers would not keep paying for expensive packs once the $400 machine's function was obviously replaceable.

author: cwyers
cardQuote: This is a case of "let's spend VC money like water to get enough customers to get a huge valuation and then figure out a business model."
quote: And how well does that work out? My experience with ad targeting is that it's mostly awful. Amazon can track every book I purchase through them, and the ads for books to buy on my Kindle are awful. Facebook has oodles of information about me, and if I turn off AdBlock for a moment there, the ads I see are... diabetes test strips (I do not have diabetes) and something involving Brook Shields that I bet is a total sham. The only online ads I see where data on me, and not just inventory, seems to play a major role is retargeting, where I look at something on Amazon and it's shown to me again in an ad in case I changed my mind about not buying it. The whole adtech industry is in awful shape, and the idea that MoviePass can be profitable by being such a periphery part of the adtech industry is laughable. People will just tell Facebook and Twitter what movies they've seen for free, there's no reason to subsidize movie tickets to get that data. This is a case of "let's spend VC money like water to get enough customers to get a huge valuation and then figure out a business model."
storyTitle: How Does MoviePass Make Money?
outcome: MoviePass shut down on September 14, 2019, after its parent company went bankrupt.
outcomeDetail: The $9.95-a-month unlimited plan burned cash on full-price tickets; the company repeatedly changed terms and restricted usage. Parent company Helios and Matheson filed for bankruptcy in January 2020.
note: The comment correctly identified the data/adtech story as a cover for a simple cash-burn model that could not survive once VC money ran out.

author: olivermarks
cardQuote: today's FT front page headline 'Wirecard relied on three opaque partners for almost all its profit'
quote: today's FT front page headline 'Wirecard relied on three opaque partners for almost all its profit' 'Dubai-based unit of German payments group was not audited' 'Al Alam Solutions, a Dubai-based payments processor with skeletal operations in the Emirate, is the largest of the three “partner” entities. The other partners are PayEasy Solutions, a Philippine payments group that shares an office with a Manila bus company, and Singapore-based Senjo. ' https://www.ft.com/content/a7b43142-6675-11e9-9adc-98bf1d35a...
storyTitle: SoftBank to invest over $1B in German payment company Wirecard
outcome: Wirecard disclosed €1.9B of missing cash in June 2020, filed for insolvency, and became one of Germany's biggest accounting scandals.
outcomeDetail: CEO Markus Braun was arrested; COO Jan Marsalek fled and was later linked to Russian intelligence. Investigators found that €1.9B supposedly held in trust accounts did not exist.
note: More than a year before the collapse, the comment highlighted the FT's reporting on opaque partner entities and Wirecard's aggressive response to journalists.

author: zachware
cardQuote: If it can't sustain its losses with free flowing capital it can't cut long-term liabilities as easily as headcount and perks (again, this is morbid), so its only option would be bankruptcy.
quote: What's so structurally fascinating, in a very morbid way, is the difference between the balance sheets of the most heavily-funded late stage companies. I have an opinion but regardless of it, if a no-asset/no-liability company is losing money and the music stops, they can cut costs and survive. It's messy but it happens. WeWork is a completely different beast. It's occupancy costs + G&A are 105% of revenue. If it can't sustain its losses with free flowing capital it can't cut long-term liabilities as easily as headcount and perks (again, this is morbid), so its only option would be bankruptcy. So in this case it would seem that the most rational way to invest in it, if you absolutely had to, would be in its debt. I have to assume, though, given this ridiculous structure, that the opco would be shielded. Man, we can't predict the future but it's pretty clear that if something does go wrong, it would be an AIG-level mess to unwind the complexities.
storyTitle: WeWork isn’t a tech company; it’s a soap opera
outcome: WeWork pulled its IPO in September 2019 and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 2023.
outcomeDetail: The S-1 revealed huge losses and Adam Neumann's self-dealing; the IPO was withdrawn and Neumann was ousted. SoftBank rescued the company, but it eventually sought bankruptcy protection in 2023.
note: Two weeks before the IPO collapse, the comment read WeWork's cost structure correctly and named bankruptcy as its only real option if capital stopped flowing.

author: du73y3ejdh
cardQuote: Quibi's premise might be new but the market they're competing in sure isnt.
quote: If you're looking for a brass tax review of Quibi this isn't it. If you're looking for a superficial analysis of Quibi in the romantically optimistic writing style endemic to today's media writers then you might enjoy it. Quibi's premise might be new but the market they're competing in sure isnt. They want users to pay for access to a catalogue that is currently a sea of garbage and unlike Netflix or YouTube they don't have the raw content volume needed to micro-target users with trash that at least suits their underserved tastes. The entire value of Quibi is the idea that media should be transitioning towards formats that favor mobile and this is something that any of the established players could copy in an instant because most of the 'tech' is just having two camera choices at all times (for portrait vs. landscape orientations).
storyTitle: Quibi Will Be a Multi-Billion Dollar Company
outcome: Quibi announced its shutdown in October 2020, about six months after launch, after raising about $1.75B.
outcomeDetail: The short-form mobile video service launched April 6, 2020, struggled to attract paying subscribers, and announced its shutdown on October 21, 2020; service ended in December. Roku later bought its content library for under $100M.
note: Written during launch week, the comment nailed the structural problem: mobile-only short video was a feature incumbents could copy, not a defensible product.

author: someperson
cardQuote: It's hard to see how the market can support so many small launch providers. That's a lot of options for what has been relatively small market.
quote: Rocket Lab, Virgin Orbit, Astra and SpaceX rideshare are all able to launch 150-500kg into orbit for a few million dollars. It's hard to see how the market can support so many small launch providers. That's a lot of options for what has been relatively small market. Rocket Lab's Peter Beck has said some of these companies are propped up by the favorable fundraising environment and to expect industry consolidation when the money runs out. Rocket Lab is obviously in a great financial position with their high launch cadence and improving re-usability technology. And SpaceX is of course in a league of their own.
storyTitle: Virgin Orbit confirms that LauncherOne has reached orbit
outcome: Virgin Orbit filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in April 2023 and sold its assets after a January 2023 launch failure.
outcomeDetail: The air-launched rocket company went public via SPAC in 2021 but had little revenue and burned cash. A failed UK launch and inability to raise new funding led to layoffs and bankruptcy.
note: The comment questioned whether the small-launch market could support so many providers, naming consolidation pressure while Virgin Orbit was still flying.

author: anonymoushn
cardQuote: Celsius is probably a scam, but the reasoning above is not why.
quote: There's no actual mechanism that matches capital to risk-adjusted returns. Reasoning as if there is reliably leads to incorrect conclusions. Celsius is probably a scam, but the reasoning above is not why.
storyTitle: The biggest crypto lending company is a ponzi scheme
outcome: Celsius froze withdrawals in June 2022 and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in July 2022; founder Alex Mashinsky was later charged with fraud.
outcomeDetail: The crypto lender had promised high yields on deposits and was among the first major firms to halt withdrawals during the 2022 crash. Its bankruptcy examiner described a chaotic, misleading operation.
note: Six months before the freeze, the comment said plainly that Celsius was probably a scam, cutting through the yield-friendly coverage.

author: steveBK123
cardQuote: I think it's the sort of white elephant project that can only thrive in a ZIRP environment. Once money has an actual cost, and investors require actual returns, there are 1000s of better business models than this.
quote: Yes. But also I think it's the sort of white elephant project that can only thrive in a ZIRP environment. Once money has an actual cost, and investors require actual returns, there are 1000s of better business models than this. Hopefully there is consolidation & regulation in the space before we have too much testing in public gone wrong. In my mind the entire self driving industry is trying to apply ML/AI practices from use cases that just require ~51%-ish "right more often than wrong" precision onto driving which needs 99.999+%. If some of your phones images are mis-tagged as a cat instead of dog, or some of your cat photos are not tagged as a cat, it's not a huge issue.. In quant trading as long as your trade makes money 51+% of the time, you are going to accumulate returns in the long run. Car license plate readers for speed tickets / tolls / etc have a similar "pretty close / pretty good" requirement.
storyTitle: Cruise driverless vehicles involved in 3 separate traffic incidents in SF
outcome: GM ended Cruise's robotaxi funding in December 2024 and folded the unit into GM, ending its driverless service.
outcomeDetail: Cruise's California permit was suspended in October 2023 after a pedestrian-dragging incident and the company's response. GM later cut spending and stopped robotaxi development.
note: The comment predicted the economics would collapse once cheap capital ended and argued AVs needed 99.999% reliability, not just better-than-average ML performance.

author: phphphphp
cardQuote: but it's also plausible that FTX is dependent upon Alameda and that Alameda's faltering could take down FTX.
quote: Hard to say, because we can only speculate on the true state of Alameda. Sam Bankman-Fried owns both Alameda and FTX and so while they’re separate entities, they are co-mingled in many ways. Assuming FTX is a profitable enterprise (a big question in the current market) then any problems Alameda faces could be addressed by SBF leveraging FTX in some way to bail Alameda out… but it’s also plausible that FTX is dependent upon Alameda and that Alameda’s faltering could take down FTX. My guess is that an Alameda implosion is unlikely because, as far as I can tell, they’re not engaging in fraudulent behaviour, just crypto hubris… and so, worst case, they have to scale back their activity… but if they are reliant on third-party capital, and the current economic trend continues… it seems plausible that could trigger major problems in the crypto world.
storyTitle: Crypto trading firm Alameda Research might be insolvent
outcome: FTX collapsed in November 2022, filed for bankruptcy, and founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud in 2023.
outcomeDetail: A run on deposits exposed that FTX had lent customer funds to Alameda Research. The exchange filed for Chapter 11 days after Binance walked away from a rescue.
note: Four days before the collapse, the comment outlined the exact Alameda-FTX contagion path, even as it hedged that fraud was unlikely.

author: verdverm
cardQuote: This thing seem dead on arrival. Who wants to hold their hand up like that? Who wants to look at an uneven "screen"?
quote: > I don't understand the insistence on using voice as the main interaction and ditching the screen. There was a google i/o talk a few years back were they talked about users wanting multi-modal, an example being they ask for restaurant recommendations by voice, then get the list they can view on their device. Both query and results are presented in their easiest modal, and humans will naturally switch between them. This thing seem dead on arrival. Who wants to hold their hand up like that? Who wants to look at an uneven "screen"? Can you use it while walking or experience the movement in a vehicle? (car, bus, subway) Is this just a big sunk cost fallacy launch?
storyTitle: Humane AI Pin
outcome: Humane's AI Pin shipped in April 2024 to scathing reviews; HP bought the company's assets in February 2025 and shut down the devices.
outcomeDetail: Reviewers criticized the Pin's latency, battery, projection and $699 price plus subscription. HP acquired Humane for about $116M, and existing pins stopped working on February 28, 2025.
note: On announcement day, the comment called the Pin dead on arrival and questioned voice-first, screenless interaction in public.

storyTitle: Northvolt develops state-of-the-art sodium-ion battery validated at 160 Wh/kg
outcome: Northvolt filed for Chapter 11 protection in November 2024 and for bankruptcy in Sweden in March 2025.
outcomeDetail: The battery maker struggled with production delays, safety issues and financing, despite billions in orders and investment. It sold assets and its founder resigned.
note: The comment dismissed Northvolt's announcements as taxpayer-funded PR, a charge that fit its later production and financial collapse.
